findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. This part works well.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable.

findings.text: This is Athena's home URL, but the title and nearly all of the body are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets one paragraph on it, then a long technical study of a tool they have never heard of.

The page says why the study is here, which helps. But the newcomer never sees what using Athena looks like: no sample of how it reads a request, its predictions, its cost record or its verdict. Those are the features the lede promises.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim

findings.text: The link to next steps is near the top, and the Next steps section gives a clone command, prerequisites, `./setup.sh` and a first command to try. That clearly answers 'what do I do next'.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself

findings.text: The prerequisites do not say whether you need a paid AI account or API key, or which models do the work and which check it, even though the lede says two different models are used. A newcomer cannot tell what it will cost them to try.
findings.source: Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code).

findings.text: This sits in the header but means nothing to a newcomer, since 'owner' and 'proposals' are not explained anywhere on the page.
findings.source: Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision.

findings.text: The firstmate terms are each defined two or three times (under 'Words used first', in the transition cards and in the Glossary), and 'in scope' is admitted to be undefined. That makes the body long and repetitive for a first-time reader.
Transition ids are used before the Transitions section defines them, and exit codes such as 75 are never explained. A newcomer reading top to bottom meets references they cannot yet follow.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: Each claim links to exact lines at a fixed commit. That is real evidence for the traceability Athena promises, and a careful newcomer can check it.
findings.source: Next steps: "Check a statement: follow a bracketed claim id to the claim, then its source link to the file and lines in firstmate at the pinned commit."
